title: How did the Inca run an empire on cloth?
teaches: Cloth as Inca state wealth; fine cumbi and everyday awasqa; labour tribute and qullqa storehouses; ritual burning and military reward; the khipu; Paracas and Wari before the Inca; Spanish obrajes and cochineal

blocks.text: In 1532 a small Spanish force under Francisco Pizarro marched inland from the coast of what is now northern Peru, into the empire of the Inca. Pizarro sent a party ahead under Hernando de Soto to the town of Caxas, in the mountains. Pizarro's secretary, Francisco de Xerez, wrote down what they reported. Caxas had storehouses full of goods, and a large building where, in his words, there were "many women spinning and weaving cloth for the army". The Spaniards saw no coins in use.

The Inca state, which called itself Tawantinsuyu, stretched about 4,000 km along the Andes, from what is now Ecuador to central Chile, and ruled perhaps ten million people. It had no money and no markets of any size. In this lesson we look at how it ran without them, and at the part cloth played: as tax, as savings, as pay, as a political gift and as an offering to the gods. The anthropologist John Murra, who first set out this argument in 1962, called cloth the main form of wealth in the Inca state.

Inca subjects did not pay taxes in goods or coin. They paid in labour, called *mit'a*: each household owed the state a share of its time, working the state's fields, building roads and terraces, serving in the army, or making things. Cloth was one of the main things made. The state handed out raw fibre, cotton from the warm coastal valleys and the wool of llamas and alpacas from the highland herds, and each household spun and wove a fixed amount of plain cloth from it and handed the cloth back. This everyday cloth was called *awasqa*.

The finest cloth, *cumbi* (also written *qompi*), was made by specialists. Some were men, the *cumbicamayoc*, who worked full time for the state. Others were women chosen as girls to live in enclosed houses, the *acllawasi*, where they wove and brewed maize beer for the state and the temples; the building at Caxas was probably one of these. Cumbi was a tapestry weave, with the weft packed so tightly that it hid the warp completely, in bright patterns of dyed alpaca and sometimes vicuña wool. Some surviving cumbi tunics have more weft threads per centimetre than most European tapestry of the same period.

Andean weaving was very old when the Inca came to power in the 15th century. At Paracas, on the south coast of Peru, a cemetery used around 2,000 years ago held mummy bundles wrapped in dozens of embroidered mantles, some with hundreds of hours of work in each. The Wari state, which ruled much of the central Andes from about 600 to 1000, made tapestry tunics with standard patterns that look like uniforms of office. The Inca inherited both the skills and the idea that a state could be run through cloth.

The cloth went into storehouses called *qullqa*, built in long rows on hillsides along the roads, where the wind kept them cool and dry. Food, weapons, sandals and cloth were stored in them. Excavated sites show how large the system was: about 500 storehouses at the provincial centre of Huánuco Pampa, about 2,000 in the hills around Hatun Xauxa, and about 2,400 at Cotapachi, in the Cochabamba valley of Bolivia, which held maize. The storehouses were connected by the **Qhapaq Ñan**, a road network of some 30,000 to 40,000 km, with two main trunk roads, one in the highlands and one along the coast.

blocks.caption: The northern and central part of the Inca empire: its two trunk roads, which ran on south into Chile, and three large storehouse sites. Paracas and Wari are older cultures whose weaving the Inca inherited.

blocks.text: Stored cloth did the work money does elsewhere. It clothed the army on campaign and the workers on state projects. It was given as a reward to soldiers and as a gift to the local lords whose loyalty the Inca needed, and a lord who received a cumbi tunic from the emperor wore the state's patterns as a sign of his rank. Fine cloth was burned as an offering at major ceremonies, sacrificed in the way other societies sacrificed animals. When the Spaniards reached Cusco in 1533, they found storehouses packed with cloth; Spanish chroniclers also report Inca commanders burning storehouses during the wars of the conquest to keep the contents from the enemy.

Running a system like this needs records: how many households in each district, how much each owed, what was in each storehouse. The Inca had no writing, but they kept accounts on the **khipu**, a set of cotton or wool cords hanging from a main cord, with knots tied along them. Specialists called *khipukamayuq* made and read them.

blocks.caption: Four pendant cords of a khipu, read as numbers. Clusters of knots nearer the main cord are thousands, hundreds and tens; a long knot at the bottom gives the units, and a figure-eight knot means one.

blocks.text: In 1912 the American historian Leland Locke showed that many khipus record numbers in a decimal system. Each cord holds one number. The position of a cluster of knots along the cord gives its place, units at the bottom, then tens, hundreds and thousands nearer the top, and a gap means zero. Tens, hundreds and thousands are shown by that many simple knots. Units use a long knot, a knot with the cord wrapped round several times, where the number of turns is the digit; a one is tied as a figure-eight knot instead, since a long knot needs at least two turns. Colours, the way cords were attached and subsidiary cords hanging from pendants added categories, such as which district or which kind of goods a number referred to. Whether khipus also recorded words, such as names, histories or songs, as Spanish chroniclers said, is still debated, and only a few hundred of the surviving examples have been studied closely.

The Spanish conquest took over parts of this system and broke the rest. The colonial government kept labour drafts, under the old name *mita*, but used them mainly to send men to the silver mines at Potosí. Tribute was now demanded in goods and silver, including cloth, which Spanish officials sold. Spanish owners set up workshops called **obrajes**, in which indigenous workers, often held there by debt or by court sentence, wove woollen cloth for the colonial market. The obrajes of Quito were the largest and were notorious for their conditions.

One Andean and Mexican dyestuff went the other way and became a global commodity. **Cochineal** is a red dye made from a scale insect that lives on prickly pear cactus. Dyers in Mexico and the Andes had used it for centuries, and Spanish merchants shipped it to Europe from the 1520s. It gave a brighter, faster red on wool and silk than any European dye, and for much of the colonial period it was one of the most valuable exports of New Spain after silver. Cochineal dyed the cardinals' robes in Rome and, later, the scarlet coats of British army officers.

**Try it.** Take three pieces of string of different colours and a longer one for the main cord. Tie the number of people in your household on one cord, the number of rooms on another, and your house number on a third, using single knots for tens and a long knot (wrap the string round several times before pulling it through) for units. Give it to someone and see whether they can read it without being told which cord is which.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the Inca and cloth.

items.ask: The Inca state had no coins. How did it pay soldiers and reward loyal local lords?
choices: With cloth and goods from its storehouses
With bars of silver from its mines
With grants of land in conquered provinces
With shells used as money across the Andes
items.why: Labour tax filled the storehouses, and stored cloth and food were handed out as pay, rewards and gifts.

items.ask: A highland household receives a bundle of alpaca wool from a state official. What is expected of it?
choices: To spin and weave a set amount of cloth
To sell the wool at the nearest market
To pay for the wool later in silver
To dye it with cochineal and keep it
items.why: The state supplied the fibre and the household supplied the labour. The tax was the work, and the product went back to the state.

items.ask: A khipu cord has 3 knots near the top, 5 lower down, and a long knot of 2 turns at the bottom. What number does it record?
items.why: Position gives the place: hundreds near the top, then tens, and the long knot at the bottom gives the units. Three hundreds, five tens and two units make 352.

items.ask: Why would an Inca army burn its own storehouses when retreating?
choices: The stores were state wealth that would supply the enemy
To signal their position to other Inca armies nearby
Burning cloth was a ritual performed at every retreat
The storehouses were too heavy to carry with them
items.why: In a state without money, stored goods were the treasury and the army's supply. Destroying them denied both to an invader.

items.ask: Why did cochineal become valuable in Europe after the 1520s?
choices: It gave a brighter, faster red than any European dye
It was the only red dye that worked on cotton
It was much cheaper than madder or kermes
Spain banned every other red dye in Europe
items.why: Cochineal's red was stronger and more lasting than Europe's own, so dyers paid a high price for it, and it became one of New Spain's leading exports.

summary: **The Inca state ran without money.** Subjects paid tax in labour, and the state stored and handed out the products.
**Cloth was the main store of wealth.** It paid soldiers, rewarded lords, marked rank and was burned as an offering.
**Two grades of cloth.** Households wove plain *awasqa* from state fibre; specialists and chosen women wove fine tapestry *cumbi*.
**Storehouses held it.** Rows of *qullqa*, up to thousands at one site, lined the roads of a network of some 30,000 to 40,000 km.
**Khipus kept the accounts.** Knotted cords recorded numbers in a decimal system by the position and type of knot.
**The skills were older than the Inca.** Paracas embroidery and Wari tapestry tunics came centuries earlier.
**The conquest redirected the system.** Labour drafts went to the silver mines, and obrajes made cloth with forced labour.
**Cochineal went global.** An American insect red became one of New Spain's most valuable exports.
